question.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.

current_example.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-2x_1x_2+2x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
current_example.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/e7d3b20a7e9d637068f5c0d9c4b62ab3d10870ef47ca7e9945f356ab2218deb4.svg)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/f5b9893c070566e26d2c1c98aebc05a868e32edc14e355863a10702f643f90f2.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/186d8f86016e321b1d83eca8e879aff51faba8e44dea80f4e68850eea3ba6e47.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/da9a30410e6abc13418b8bfaa5a3edfa174be89e76d3fc5962afade37ca45d21.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/d1fb817fbad49dfb983477b5b9ebdecbd65054b0bdff330d84ca8fbad75d5e5c.svg)

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/78e9f7751c5fc058b75e91677b6fdaebdcb3e1b51988c83dd22bb9741e548f7d.svg)
